title: Many ways of being Sikh
hookLine: amritdhari, keshdhari, sahajdhari: people live their Sikhi at many stages, and the Gurus welcomed seekers
last: AMRIT SANCHAR — A STEP, NOT A PRESSURE.

lines: A TURBAN, A PATKA, SHORT HAIR, A GUEST.
cards: Sunday, the langar hall of a gurdwara, and the row on the floor is a mix. One man wears a tall blue turban and a steel kara, and took amrit years ago.

Next to him, his nephew, uncut hair tied under a patka, still thinking about amrit. Across the row, a woman with short hair who sings every hymn by heart. A college student, here with a friend for the first time.
Same floor, same food. Today: many ways of being Sikh.

teach.b: Back on day one hundred thirty-nine, at the gurdwara door, the short answer was: start where you are. Today, the words Sikhs use for it.
Sikh itself means a learner, a disciple, usually traced to the same old root as the Sanskrit shishya, a student. So the name assumes you're somewhere along the way, not finished.
Sikhs often use three words for where people are.
Amritdhari: one who has taken amrit and keeps the full discipline. Keshdhari: one who keeps uncut hair but hasn't yet taken amrit.
And sahajdhari, usually explained from sahaj, ease or gradualness: one who walks the path at their own pace, often without the outward forms. You'll also hear mona, for a Sikh who cuts their hair.

teach.h: SIKHS DEBATE WHERE THE LINES FALL.
teach.b: Sikhs don't all agree on how these words should be used. The Sikh code of conduct defines a Sikh by belief: in one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib, and the tenth Guru's amrit.
How far the word stretches is a live debate, and in recent decades it has even reached the courts in India. What nobody disputes is where the Gurus began. Guru Nanak sat with anyone.
The Guru Granth Sahib includes voices from beyond the Gurus' own line: Muslim and Hindu saints, a weaver, a leatherworker. The langar feeds whoever walks in.

teach.h: THE GURUS KEPT AN OPEN DOOR.
teach.b: The Gurus built a house with an open door. So the everyday question isn't, am I Sikh enough?
It's the learner's question: what's my next step? For one person it's amrit. For another, learning to read Gurmukhi.
For a guest, maybe just sitting on the floor and eating.

how: Sikhs speak of amritdhari (initiated), keshdhari (keeping uncut hair) and sahajdhari Sikhs; gurdwaras welcome everyone to the sangat and the langar, whatever their stage or background.

o: a Sikh who walks the path at their own pace
a Sikh who lives as a wandering ascetic
a Sikh family's chosen household teacher

games.q: the words for where people are — tap the pairs.
p: keeps uncut hair, not yet initiated
walks the path at their own pace

s: it shares an old root with the Sanskrit shishya, a student.
Sikhs all agree exactly who counts as a Sikh
how far the word stretches is debated, and has even reached courts in India.
the Guru Granth Sahib includes only the Gurus' own hymns
it also holds hymns by Hindu and Muslim saints, including a weaver and a leatherworker.

games.q: a first-time visitor to a gurdwara, not Sikh, wonders if they're allowed to eat at langar. what does the tradition say?
o: only initiated Sikhs may eat there.
anyone who walks in is fed, on the same floor.
guests eat separately, after the Sikhs.
games.why: langar feeds whoever comes, seated together. the Gurus built it as an open door.

practice: Place yourself in that langar hall, exactly as you are today, whatever you believe, whatever you're unsure of. If a voice in you says you're too early, too late or not enough, let it be there, and let it quiet down.
Then ask the learner's question gently, what's one next step for me in anything that matters, and hold the answer lightly.

wordCard.voice: Sahajdhari, one who walks at their own pace. Sikh means learner; amritdhari, keshdhari, sahajdhari: people live their Sikhi at many stages, and the Gurus welcomed seekers.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sikh, a learner or disciple; related to the Sanskrit shishya, a student.

carryVoice: Your line: every seeker welcome. Sikh means learner, and a learner is never finished. Day two hundred seventy-two, done.
